title: The Turning Point: miután and mielőtt Together

sections.title: Marking the moment everything changes
sections.content: A story's turning point often needs both directions at once: what had just finished (miután) and what was still to come (mielőtt), pinned around the one event that changes everything. Stack them in a single sentence, or across two short sentences — either works, as long as the order of clauses matches the order you want the reader to picture.

items.spanish: Miután végzett a munkával, mielőtt hazament, még beugrott a boltba.
items.english: After he finished work, before he went home, he still popped into the shop.

items.spanish: Miután mindenki elaludt, mielőtt megvirradt, valaki halkan kinyitotta az ajtót.
items.english: After everyone had fallen asleep, before dawn broke, someone quietly opened the door.

items.spanish: Miután becsukta az ajtót, mielőtt leült, még egyszer körülnézett a szobában.
items.english: After she closed the door, before she sat down, she looked around the room once more.

sections.content: Two subordinate clauses stacked in front of one main clause is a genuinely advanced move — use it exactly where a story needs it, at the hinge moment, and go back to one clause at a time everywhere else. A whole story told entirely in miután…, mielőtt…, sentences reads as breathless, not skilled.
